step.detail:
Question: When can someone complain to HDC, what process stages and time limits are stated, and what outcomes are possible? Quote the key lines.
Anyone can complain to HDC, and “If issues persist, or if the above options are not suitable for you, you can complain to the HDC.” The page says the process can involve assessment, asking the provider to sort it out, referral to another agency, closing the complaint, or a formal investigation; it may take “only a few days or a year or more,” and formal investigations “often… takes about two years.” Possible outcomes include apology, changes/recommendations, sending the complaint to an advocate, sending it to the provider or another organisation, or a formal investigation; very rarely, a Director of Proceedings referral follows a breach finding.

step.detail:
Question: How does HDC say to make a complaint, what should happen first if anything, and what timing or information requirements are given? Quote the key lines.
HDC says to complete the online complaint form, though complaints by post are still accepted and you can also call 0800 11 22 33 or get help from the Advocacy Service. As a first step, HDC suggests you speak directly to your provider because it is “often the quickest and easiest way to resolve your complaint.” Before filling out the form, you need key information such as your contact details, NHI number, provider details, incident details, supporting documents, and if complaining for someone else, evidence of consent or legal authority; if the form is not completed it cannot be saved.

ACC says weekly compensation is financial support that helps replace part of your income so you’ll still get paid while you recover. If you qualify, you usually became eligible on day 8 after your injury; if it isn’t your first time off work for the same injury, or it’s for approved surgery, payment may be available straight away. step.detail:
Question: What national timeframes under Right 10 does this page give for acknowledging, deciding, and informing a complainant? Quote the key lines.
The page says a provider must acknowledge a complaint in writing within 5 working days, make a decision within 10 working days of written acknowledgement, and inform the consumer of the decision “as soon as practicable” after the decision is made. It also says that if more than 20 additional working days will be needed, the provider must inform the consumer within the 10-working-day timeframe. There must never be more than one calendar month between communications.
✓ quote found in the page: "A provider must acknowledge any complaint in writing within 5 working days (Right 10(6)(a))."
✓ quote found in the page: "A decision on whether the complaint is justified or not, or whether more time is needed to investigate the complaint, must be made by the provider within 10 working days of giving written acknowledgement of receipt of the complaint (Right 10(7))."
✓ quote found in the page: "If the decision is that more time is needed to investigate the complaint, and that more than 20 additional working days will be required, the provider must inform the consumer of that (with reasons) within the 10 working days timeframe (Right 10(7)(b)(ii))."
✓ quote found in the page: "If the decision is whether or not the complaint is justified, the consumer must be informed of that decision (with reasons, any proposed actions, and any appeal procedure) “as soon as practicable” after making the decision (Right 10(8))."

Question: How do you get legal aid, can you check eligibility online, and who applies? Quote the key lines.

Question: Who publishes this guideline page, what service or hospital is it from, and what does it say about suspected scaphoid fractures? Quote the key lines.
It is published by Starship clinical guidelines / Starship Child Health, from Starship Child Health (Starship Hospital). For suspected scaphoid fractures, the page says to diagnose by clinical suspicion when the x-ray is negative and manage in a scaphoid splint with fracture-clinic follow-up in 10–14 days. It also notes that only a small percentage are true fractures on follow-up, and that in children under 10 wrist splints are sufficient when a fracture is suspected but not visible on imaging.

step.detail:
Question: What does this policy say about treatment injury cover, exclusions, and any timing points for lodging or cover? Quote the key lines.
The policy says ACC covers treatment injury for claims lodged on or after 1 July 2005 after receiving treatment from a registered health professional, and before 1 July 2005 it is assessed under medical misadventure. It excludes injuries that are a necessary part or ordinary consequence of treatment, solely attributable to a resource allocation decision, or where the treatment did not achieve the desired result. Timing points include that the date of injury is when the client first seeks or receives treatment for the symptoms, and cover can be available for failure to provide treatment or to provide treatment in a timely manner if earlier treatment would have prevented or lessened the injury.

The factsheet says rule 6 requests “must be dealt with promptly” and agencies should respond “as soon as possible but within 20 working days,” or transfer the request “within ten working days” if it belongs to another agency. step.detail:
Question: How does a treatment injury claim get lodged, who lodges it, and what forms are used? Quote the key lines.
A registered provider lodges the claim on behalf of the patient, and the best way is to use a practice management system (PMS) or ACC’s online system. For treatment injury, the provider ticks the “is this claim for treatment injury” box on the ACC45; all providers other than dentists use an ACC45, while dentists use an ACC42. The page also says the patient or authorised representative must consent, and the provider must record that consent.

step.detail:
Question: What does this official legislation page say about bringing proceedings for personal injury independently of the Act? Quote the key lines.
The page says that a person may bring proceedings for personal injury independently of the Act in limited circumstances: if the claimant has cover for the injury, the person can bring proceedings only for exemplary damages, and if the claimant has no cover, the proceedings are not barred by the Act. It also says proceedings brought independently of the Act do not affect a claimant's right to entitlements. The key section is 317, and the surrounding provisions at 318–321 explain related limits and ACC's role.

Question: How does a patient at Auckland City Hospital request records, by what methods, and what identification or consent is required? Quote the key lines.
A patient can request their own or a dependant’s records by completing the request form, providing the requested identification, and then emailing or posting it. For another person’s record, written consent is required if the person is a family member who is not a dependant (16 years or under). The page says identification requirements are on page three of the form.

✓ quote found in the page: "Identification requirements are on page three of the form."

✓ quote found in the page: "Please note: If the request is for the clinical record of a family member who is not a dependant (16 years or under) then that person's consent is required in writing."

This page only shows the contents list, not the text of section 53, so it does not say what the time limit is or when ACC must accept a late claim. It does show that the relevant section is “53 Time for making claim” and that “58 Effect of failure to meet time limits” is a separate section. Question: What does ACC say about asking for an independent review, by when, and how? Quote the key lines.
ACC says you can apply for a review of decisions about your claim or levy invoice if you disagree with them. You need to apply within three months of the decision, and you can apply by filling in the review application or writing a letter, then emailing or posting it. If you’re sending a letter, ACC says to include your details, the claim/ACC number, the decision date, why you want a review, and any supporting documents.

Question: How do you apply to the Accident Compensation Appeals Tribunal, what must happen first, and what time limit is stated? Quote the key lines.
You apply by filling in the Notice of Appeal form and sending it to the Accident Compensation Appeals District Court Registry. Question: What does HDC say about raising concerns directly with a provider first, and what practical steps does it suggest? Quote the key lines.
HDC says you should first work directly with the person or organisation that provided the service, because it can help resolve concerns more quickly and may get you an explanation or apology. Question: What does HDC say about referring complaints back to providers, to advocates, or to other agencies? Quote the key lines.
HDC says it may ask the provider to sort out the complaint with the help of the Advocacy Service, refer the complaint to another agency better placed to handle it, or send it to an advocate or the provider to sort out. It also says HDC can refer complaints to other organisations better placed to help, such as the Privacy Commissioner or a District Inspector.

steps.body: Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora Auckland | Te Toka Tumai
steps.what: Auckland City Hospital is a public hospital service run by Health New Zealand Te Toka Tumai Auckland. For complaints about emergency department care, Health NZ says to raise the concern with the service first if you can, then use the Auckland Central feedback/complaint form or the Consumer Feedback Team.
points: Auckland City Hospital is a public hospital service run by this provider.
Health NZ says working with the service provider directly is the fastest route, and the Auckland page says to speak to staff or the manager first if possible.
Under the provider’s current page, complaints are acknowledged within 5 working days and the provider aims to complete the investigation within 20 working days.
Under Right 10 nationally, the provider must decide within 10 working days of written acknowledgement whether the complaint is justified or whether more time is needed.
If more than 20 additional working days are needed, the provider must tell the consumer within that 10-working-day period and give reasons.
Health NZ says complaints are confidential and are not added to the clinical record.
steps.appliesIf: Public hospital care at Auckland City Hospital / Health New Zealand Te Toka Tumai Auckland.
alternatives: Phone the Consumer Feedback Team on 09 375 7048.
Email feedback.auckland@tewhatuora.govt.nz.
Post to Consumer Feedback Team, Health New Zealand Te Toka Tumai Auckland, Private Bag 92024, Auckland Mail Centre, Auckland 1142.
If still unhappy, complain to the Health and Disability Commissioner.
missing: Which Auckland City Hospital service to name on the form (for example Emergency Department).
The names or roles of staff involved, if known.
What outcome the patient wants.

steps.body: Health and Disability Commissioner
steps.what: If the hospital’s answer is not good enough, or if complaining directly is not suitable, the independent route is the Health and Disability Commissioner (HDC). HDC has an online complaint form, but it strongly suggests trying the provider first because that is often quickest.
steps.deadline: "The earlier you raise your concerns, the more straightforward they can be to resolve."
points: Anyone can complain to HDC.
HDC suggests speaking directly to the provider first, but this is not an absolute precondition if that route is not suitable.
The online complaint route starts with a wizard asking whether you are complaining on behalf of someone else.

Before using HDC’s online form, you should gather your contact details, provider details, NHI number, incident details, supporting documents, and any consent or authority if complaining for someone else.
HDC may ask the provider to sort the complaint out with you, send it to an advocate, or refer it to another agency such as the Privacy Commissioner.
HDC says complaint handling can take only a few days or a year or more, and a formal investigation often takes about two years.
requires: Usually, HDC suggests you speak directly to your provider first.
alternatives: Ask the Nationwide Health and Disability Advocacy Service for help first.
Complain to the provider directly through Health New Zealand’s Auckland Central feedback route.
missing: Whether the patient wants to complain only for themself or on behalf of someone else.
NHI number, if available.
Provider details, dates, and supporting documents.

steps.body: Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora Auckland | Te Toka Tumai
steps.what: Auckland City Hospital is a public hospital service run by Health New Zealand Te Toka Tumai Auckland. For complaints about emergency department care, Health NZ says to raise the concern with the service first if you can, then use the Auckland Central feedback/complaint form or the Consumer Feedback Team.
points: Auckland City Hospital is a public hospital service run by this provider.
Health NZ says working with the service provider directly is the fastest route, and the Auckland page says to speak to staff or the manager first if possible.
Under the provider’s current page, complaints are acknowledged within 5 working days and the provider aims to complete the investigation within 20 working days.
Under Right 10 nationally, the provider must decide within 10 working days of written acknowledgement whether the complaint is justified or whether more time is needed.
If more than 20 additional working days are needed, the provider must tell the consumer within that 10-working-day period and give reasons.
Health NZ says complaints are confidential and are not added to the clinical record.
steps.appliesIf: Public hospital care at Auckland City Hospital / Health New Zealand Te Toka Tumai Auckland.
alternatives: Phone the Consumer Feedback Team on 09 375 7048.
Email feedback.auckland@tewhatuora.govt.nz.
Post to Consumer Feedback Team, Health New Zealand Te Toka Tumai Auckland, Private Bag 92024, Auckland Mail Centre, Auckland 1142.
If still unhappy, complain to the Health and Disability Commissioner.

steps.body: Health and Disability Commissioner
steps.what: If the hospital’s answer is not good enough, or if complaining directly is not suitable, the independent route is the Health and Disability Commissioner (HDC). HDC has an online complaint form, but it strongly suggests trying the provider first because that is often quickest.
steps.deadline: "The earlier you raise your concerns, the more straightforward they can be to resolve."
points: Anyone can complain to HDC.
HDC suggests speaking directly to the provider first, but this is not an absolute precondition if that route is not suitable.
The online complaint route starts with a wizard asking whether you are complaining on behalf of someone else.

Before using HDC’s online form, you should gather your contact details, provider details, NHI number, incident details, supporting documents, and any consent or authority if complaining for someone else.
HDC may ask the provider to sort the complaint out with you, send it to an advocate, or refer it to another agency such as the Privacy Commissioner.
HDC says complaint handling can take only a few days or a year or more, and a formal investigation often takes about two years.
requires: Usually, HDC suggests you speak directly to your provider first.
alternatives: Ask the Nationwide Health and Disability Advocacy Service for help first.
Complain to the provider directly through Health New Zealand’s Auckland Central feedback route.
missing: Whether the patient wants to complain only for themself or on behalf of someone else.
NHI number, if available.
Provider details, dates, and supporting documents.

sources.quote: Anyone can make a complaint to HDC.
If issues persist, or if the above options are not suitable for you, you can complain to the HDC.
As a first step, we suggest you speak directly to your provider.
Are you complaining on behalf of someone else?
Ask the provider to sort out your complaint with you, with the help of the Advocacy Service.
It may take only a few days or a year or more.

points: The service is free.

It helps people understand their rights, discuss concerns, talk through options, and make a complaint.
Contact is available by freephone, email, and live chat via its website.
alternatives: Complain directly to Health New Zealand Te Toka Tumai Auckland.
Complain to the Health and Disability Commissioner.

steps.body: Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC)
steps.what: For harm caused by treatment in New Zealand public care, the main compensation route is ACC’s no-fault treatment injury scheme, not a negligence damages claim. A registered provider lodges the treatment injury claim for the patient, and if ACC later declines cover or entitlements there is an internal-independent review route and then an appeal route.
points: ACC says a treatment injury is a personal injury caused by treatment from a registered health professional.
To be covered, the injury must involve physical harm or damage and must not be a necessary part or ordinary consequence of the treatment.
For lost earnings, ACC says weekly compensation may be available from day 8 and may pay up to 80% of pre-injury income.

New Zealand legislation says damages proceedings for covered personal injury are barred independently of the Act, so court damages are not the normal route; exemplary damages are the narrow exception if applicable.
requires: A registered provider to lodge the claim on the patient’s behalf.
Patient consent or authorised representative consent for the provider to lodge it.
steps.appliesIf: Personal injury caused by treatment from a registered health professional in New Zealand.
alternatives: A complaint to Health New Zealand or HDC can run alongside ACC, but is separate from compensation.
Court damages are generally barred for covered personal injury, except for limited proceedings such as exemplary damages.
missing: Which clinician will lodge the treatment injury claim now.
Whether the patient has had wage loss from surgery or inability to work.
Any ACC decision letter, if a claim is later declined or limited.

steps.body: Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC)
steps.what: For harm caused by treatment in New Zealand public care, the main compensation route is ACC’s no-fault treatment injury scheme, not a negligence damages claim. A registered provider lodges the treatment injury claim for the patient, and if ACC later declines cover or entitlements there is an internal-independent review route and then an appeal route.
points: ACC says a treatment injury is a personal injury caused by treatment from a registered health professional.
To be covered, the injury must involve physical harm or damage and must not be a necessary part or ordinary consequence of the treatment.
For lost earnings, ACC says weekly compensation may be available from day 8 and may pay up to 80% of pre-injury income.

New Zealand legislation says damages proceedings for covered personal injury are barred independently of the Act, so court damages are not the normal route; exemplary damages are the narrow exception if applicable.
requires: A registered provider to lodge the claim on the patient’s behalf.
Patient consent or authorised representative consent for the provider to lodge it.
steps.appliesIf: Personal injury caused by treatment from a registered health professional in New Zealand.
alternatives: A complaint to Health New Zealand or HDC can run alongside ACC, but is separate from compensation.
Court damages are generally barred for covered personal injury, except for limited proceedings such as exemplary damages.
missing: Which clinician will lodge the treatment injury claim now.
Whether the patient has had wage loss from surgery or inability to work.
Any ACC decision letter, if a claim is later declined or limited.

not be a necessary part or ordinary consequence of the treatment.

points: The Ministry of Justice says civil legal aid may be available for civil disputes or problems that could go to court or a tribunal.
Eligibility for civil legal aid depends on income, assets, merits, and any arrears from a previous legal aid debt.

For family or civil legal aid, the first step is to find a legal aid lawyer, and the lawyer helps with the application form; no online checker or online application was found on the official pages reviewed.

steps.body: Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora Auckland | Te Toka Tumai
steps.what: Auckland City Hospital is a public hospital service run by Health New Zealand Te Toka Tumai Auckland. For complaints about emergency department care, Health NZ says to raise the concern with the service first if you can, then use the Auckland Central feedback/complaint form or the Consumer Feedback Team.
points: Auckland City Hospital is a public hospital service run by this provider.
Health NZ says working with the service provider directly is the fastest route, and the Auckland page says to speak to staff or the manager first if possible.
Under the provider’s current page, complaints are acknowledged within 5 working days and the provider aims to complete the investigation within 20 working days.
Under Right 10 nationally, the provider must decide within 10 working days of written acknowledgement whether the complaint is justified or whether more time is needed.
If more than 20 additional working days are needed, the provider must tell the consumer within that 10-working-day period and give reasons.
Health NZ says complaints are confidential and are not added to the clinical record.
steps.appliesIf: Public hospital care at Auckland City Hospital / Health New Zealand Te Toka Tumai Auckland.
alternatives: Phone the Consumer Feedback Team on 09 375 7048.
Email feedback.auckland@tewhatuora.govt.nz.
Post to Consumer Feedback Team, Health New Zealand Te Toka Tumai Auckland, Private Bag 92024, Auckland Mail Centre, Auckland 1142.
If still unhappy, complain to the Health and Disability Commissioner.
missing: Which Auckland City Hospital service to name on the form (for example Emergency Department).
The names or roles of staff involved, if known.
What outcome the patient wants.

steps.body: Health and Disability Commissioner
steps.what: If the hospital’s answer is not good enough, or if complaining directly is not suitable, the independent route is the Health and Disability Commissioner (HDC). HDC has an online complaint form, but it strongly suggests trying the provider first because that is often quickest.
steps.deadline: "The earlier you raise your concerns, the more straightforward they can be to resolve."
points: Anyone can complain to HDC.
HDC suggests speaking directly to the provider first, but this is not an absolute precondition if that route is not suitable.
The online complaint route starts with a wizard asking whether you are complaining on behalf of someone else.

Before using HDC’s online form, you should gather your contact details, provider details, NHI number, incident details, supporting documents, and any consent or authority if complaining for someone else.
HDC may ask the provider to sort the complaint out with you, send it to an advocate, or refer it to another agency such as the Privacy Commissioner.
HDC says complaint handling can take only a few days or a year or more, and a formal investigation often takes about two years.
requires: Usually, HDC suggests you speak directly to your provider first.
alternatives: Ask the Nationwide Health and Disability Advocacy Service for help first.
Complain to the provider directly through Health New Zealand’s Auckland Central feedback route.
missing: Whether the patient wants to complain only for themself or on behalf of someone else.
NHI number, if available.
Provider details, dates, and supporting documents.

sources.quote: Anyone can make a complaint to HDC.
If issues persist, or if the above options are not suitable for you, you can complain to the HDC.
As a first step, we suggest you speak directly to your provider.
Are you complaining on behalf of someone else?
Ask the provider to sort out your complaint with you, with the help of the Advocacy Service.
It may take only a few days or a year or more.

steps.body: Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC)
steps.what: For treatment-related harm in New Zealand, ACC is the official compensation route. A registered provider can lodge the claim for the patient, and if ACC later makes a decision the patient disagrees with, there is a review route and then an appeal route.
steps.deadline: "You need to apply for a review within three months of our decision."
points: ACC says a treatment injury is a personal injury caused by treatment from a registered health professional.
To be covered, the injury must involve physical harm or damage.
It must also not be a necessary part or ordinary consequence of the treatment.
A registered provider can lodge the claim on behalf of the patient, and the best way is through a practice management system or ACC’s online system.
Weekly compensation may pay up to 80% of pre-injury income.
If ACC makes a decision you disagree with, you need to apply for a review within three months of the decision.
requires: A registered provider to lodge the claim on the patient’s behalf.
steps.appliesIf: Personal injury caused by treatment from a registered health professional in New Zealand.
alternatives: ACC alternative dispute resolution, which can include mediation, conciliation, and facilitation.
Appeal to the Accident Compensation Appeals District Court Registry after an ACC decision, within the appeal time limit on the Ministry of Justice page.
missing: Which provider will lodge the ACC treatment injury claim now.
Whether the patient has wage loss or needs weekly compensation.

sources.quote: A treatment injury is a personal injury caused from treatment provided by a registered health professional.
involve physical harm or damage
not be a necessary part or ordinary consequence of the treatment.
As a registered provider, you can lodge claims on behalf of your patient if you think they have an injury we cover.
The best and most efficient way to lodge a patient's claim is to use a practice management system (PMS) or our online system.
You may get up to 80% of the income you earned before your injury, before tax and deductions.

steps.what: For an adult in New Zealand, the official pages reviewed do not show legal aid for the initial ACC treatment injury claim itself, which is provider-lodged, but civil legal aid may be available for disputes that could go to a court or tribunal. Lawyers may use conditional-fee ('no win no fee') agreements in some work, but the official pages reviewed do not state a success-fee cap.
points: The Ministry of Justice says civil legal aid may be available for civil disputes or problems that could go to court or a tribunal.
Eligibility for civil legal aid depends on income, assets, merits, and any arrears from a previous legal aid debt.

For family or civil legal aid, the first step is to find a legal aid lawyer, and the lawyer helps with the application form; no online checker or online application was found on the official pages reviewed.
The Law Society says a conditional fee agreement must be in writing and include certain details.
The Law Society page reviewed does not state any cap on conditional fees or success percentages.
For ACC reviews, ACC says it pays for the costs of an independent review and may also pay other review-related costs such as travel to the hearing.
requires: For legal aid, a dispute that could go to a court or tribunal and a legal aid lawyer to submit the application.
For ACC review-cost help, there must already be an ACC decision under review.
steps.appliesIf: Adult needing funding for an ACC treatment-injury dispute, review or appeal in New Zealand.
alternatives: Conditional-fee agreement with a lawyer if offered.

ACC review route, where ACC says it pays the independent review costs.

Your first step is to find a legal aid lawyer you want to advise and represent you.

a conditional fee (based on success) – a conditional fee agreement must be in writing and must include certain details², such as the way the fee will be determined and when and how the fee will be payable.

steps.what: The official profession-run way to find a lawyer is the New Zealand Law Society’s 'Find a lawyer' directory, with the Law Society registry lookup used to check details. You can search by location and area of law, then verify the lawyer on the register.

points: ACC says a treatment injury is a personal injury caused by treatment from a registered health professional.

Weekly compensation may pay up to 80% of pre-injury income.

Patient clinical record requests — Auckland (North and West) (https://www.healthnz.govt.nz/hospitals-services/hospitals/auckland/north-west/clinical-records)
A patient can request their own record or a dependant’s record by completing the request form and then emailing it, bringing it in, or posting it to the Clinical records department. The page says to provide the requested identification depending on whose information you are requesting, and that the identification requirements are on page 3 of the form. For mental health treatment records, complete the form and send it in; for another person’s record, written consent is required if they are not your dependant.

says.detail:
Make a complaint — Health & Disability Commissioner (https://www.hdc.org.nz/making-a-complaint/make-a-complaint/)
HDC says to complete the online complaint form, though complaints by post are still accepted and you can also call 0800 11 22 33 or get help from the Advocacy Service. As a first step, HDC suggests you speak directly to your provider because it is “often the quickest and easiest way to resolve your complaint.” Before filling out the form, you need key information such as your contact details, NHI number, provider details, incident details, supporting documents, and if complaining for someone else, evidence of consent or legal authority; if the form is not completed it cannot be saved.
Quotes: "As a first step, we suggest you speak directly to your provider." | "To help our team accurately assess your complaint, we ask that you complete our online complaint form." | "Before filling out the online form you will need" | "Please note — if the form is not completed it cannot be saved."

says.detail:
Fracture - scaphoid fractures (https://starship.org.nz/guidelines/fracture-clinic-scaphoid-fractures/?redirect=true)
It is published by Starship clinical guidelines / Starship Child Health, from Starship Child Health (Starship Hospital). For suspected scaphoid fractures, the page says to diagnose by clinical suspicion when the x-ray is negative and manage in a scaphoid splint with fracture-clinic follow-up in 10–14 days. The policy says ACC covers treatment injury for claims lodged on or after 1 July 2005 after receiving treatment from a registered health professional, and before 1 July 2005 it is assessed under medical misadventure. says.detail:
Review application - ACC33 (https://www.acc.co.nz/im-injured/resolve-an-issue/apply-for-a-review-acc33)
The route is a formal, independent review process: you submit the ACC33 form, ACC first tries to resolve the issue with you, and if there’s no agreement an independent reviewer is assigned to hold a hearing and issue a decision. The form asks for your contact details plus information about the review, including details of the ACC decision, your reasons for disputing it, and any supporting information; the page also shows the first step asks whether you’re applying for yourself, as an authorised contact, or acting for someone else. says.text: Complain: Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora Auckland | Te Toka Tumai. Auckland City Hospital is a public hospital service run by Health New Zealand Te Toka Tumai Auckland. For complaints about emergency department care, Health NZ says to raise the concern with the service first if you can, then use the Auckland Central feedback/complaint form or the Consumer Feedback Team. (one official source)

If that fails: Health and Disability Commissioner. If the hospital’s answer is not good enough, or if complaining directly is not suitable, the independent route is the Health and Disability Commissioner (HDC). HDC has an online complaint form, but it strongly suggests trying the provider first because that is often quickest. (not confirmed yet)

Free help: Nationwide Health and Disability Advocacy Service. Free independent help is available from the Nationwide Health and Disability Advocacy Service. It can explain your rights, help you raise concerns, and support you with a complaint against the hospital or alongside an HDC complaint. (one official source)

Your records: Health New Zealand | Te Whatu Ora Auckland Central clinical records department. To get records from Auckland City Hospital, use the Release of personal health information request form, add the requested identification, and send it to the Auckland Central clinical records department. National privacy rules say they must respond as soon as possible and within 20 working days. (not confirmed yet)

Compensation: Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC). For harm caused by treatment in New Zealand public care, the main compensation route is ACC’s no-fault treatment injury scheme, not a negligence damages claim. A registered provider lodges the treatment injury claim for the patient, and if ACC later declines cover or entitlements there is an internal-independent review route and then an appeal route. (not confirmed yet)

Paying for help: New Zealand Ministry of Justice / New Zealand Law Society / ACC. For an adult in New Zealand, the official pages reviewed do not show legal aid for the initial ACC treatment injury claim itself, which is provider-lodged, but civil legal aid may be available for disputes that could go to a court or tribunal. Lawyers may use conditional-fee ('no win no fee') agreements in some work, but the official pages reviewed do not state a success-fee cap. (not confirmed yet)

Finding a lawyer: New Zealand Law Society. The official profession-run way to find a lawyer is the New Zealand Law Society’s 'Find a lawyer' directory, with the Law Society registry lookup used to check details. You can search by location and area of law, then verify the lawyer on the register.

Clinical guidance: Starship Child Health, part of Health New Zealand Te Whatu Ora Te Toka Tumai (Auckland). The only accessible Auckland scaphoid-fracture clinical guideline found in this run is published by Starship Child Health, which is part of Health New Zealand Te Toka Tumai Auckland. It is a Starship clinical guideline, so it is an official Auckland guideline source, but it is a paediatric service source rather than clear proof of the adult Auckland City Hospital ED’s exact guideline set. (not confirmed yet)

says.text: Compensation: Accident Compensation Corporation (ACC). For treatment-related harm in New Zealand, ACC is the official compensation route. A registered provider can lodge the claim for the patient, and if ACC later makes a decision the patient disagrees with, there is a review route and then an appeal route. (not confirmed yet)

Auckland City Hospital is a public Health New Zealand hospital, so complaints start with Health NZ Te Toka Tumai Auckland and can then go to the independent Health and Disability Commissioner if needed. For compensation for treatment harm, New Zealand uses ACC’s treatment-injury scheme rather than an ordinary damages claim, and your records can be requested directly from Auckland Central clinical records using Health NZ’s form.

Question: How does HDC say to make a complaint, what should happen first if anything, and what timing or information requirements are given? Quote the key lines.
HDC says to complete the online complaint form, though complaints by post are still accepted and you can also call 0800 11 22 33 or get help from the Advocacy Service. As a first step, HDC suggests you speak directly to your provider because it is “often the quickest and easiest way to resolve your complaint.” Before filling out the form, you need key information such as your contact details, NHI number, provider details, incident details, supporting documents, and if complaining for someone else, evidence of consent or legal authority; if the form is not completed it cannot be saved.

trace.detail:
Question: What national timeframes under Right 10 does this page give for acknowledging, deciding, and informing a complainant? Quote the key lines.
The page says a provider must acknowledge a complaint in writing within 5 working days, make a decision within 10 working days of written acknowledgement, and inform the consumer of the decision “as soon as practicable” after the decision is made. It also says that if more than 20 additional working days will be needed, the provider must inform the consumer within the 10-working-day timeframe. There must never be more than one calendar month between communications.

Question: What does Right 10 say about the right to complain and any complaint procedure requirements? Quote the key lines.
Right 10 says every consumer has the right to complain in any form appropriate to the consumer, and providers must have and follow complaint procedures that are fair, simple, speedy, and efficient. The procedure must acknowledge the complaint in writing within 5 working days unless resolved, tell the consumer about internal and external complaint options, document the complaint and actions, provide relevant information, and give a decision within 10 working days of acknowledgment (or explain any longer investigation).

Question: What does this policy say about treatment injury cover, exclusions, and any timing points for lodging or cover? Quote the key lines.
The policy says ACC covers treatment injury for claims lodged on or after 1 July 2005 after receiving treatment from a registered health professional, and before 1 July 2005 it is assessed under medical misadventure. It excludes injuries that are a necessary part or ordinary consequence of treatment, solely attributable to a resource allocation decision, or where the treatment did not achieve the desired result. Timing points include that the date of injury is when the client first seeks or receives treatment for the symptoms, and cover can be available for failure to provide treatment or to provide treatment in a timely manner if earlier treatment would have prevented or lessened the injury.
